ch01.note: Zhang Fang and his men are biaoshi, the armed guards of an escort agency (biaoju)—a real institution of the period, professionals who convoyed silver, goods and travellers through bandit country for a fee. Having just delivered their cargo and been paid off, they are flush with money and off their guard.

Old money and weight. A wen or ‘cash’ was the low-value copper coin of daily life, strung together by the hundred; a liang or tael (the monk’s silver, below) was a far larger silver unit. A jin or catty is a weight of about 600 grams. Ten cash a catty is street-vendor cheap.

Tang chao lizi: chestnuts stir-roasted in a wok with sugar and coarse grit until glossy and sweet, still sold hot from a barrow on cold streets today—a homely, reassuring thing for a poisoner to be selling.

Mandarin ducks (yuanyang), thought to pair for life, are the stock emblem of wedded love and the natural thing to embroider on a bride’s red shoes. An owl in their place is a pointed reversal: in Chinese folk belief the owl is a bird of ill omen, a harbinger of death.

More old units of measure. A cun or ‘inch’ is about 3 cm, so the plank is a good hand’s-breadth thick; a zhang (just below) is ten chi, roughly 3.3 metres, so a leap of four zhang clears some thirteen metres; a li (the ‘thousand li’ of the next vignette) is about half a kilometre, and ‘a thousand li’ is the stock phrase for a very great distance.

Qinggong, ‘lightness-skill’: the martial discipline, taken for granted throughout wuxia fiction, of moving as though almost weightless—leaping rooftops, running up walls, skimming across water. The shabby, humble monk who proves to be a lethal master is itself a stock figure; the Shaolin monastery is the archetypal home of such fighting monks, though this one’s sect is never named.

A huo pusa or ‘living Bodhisattva’ is a common term of praise for one of great mercy—a Bodhisattva being an enlightened being who remains in the world to save others. The passengers mean it in earnest; the reader, who has just watched the monk beg pardon for a single lie and then kill eight men in the night, is meant to feel the irony.

ch01.anchor: What Ximen Chuixue blows from his sword is not snow
ch01.note: A play on the name. Ximen is a two-syllable surname; the given name Chuixue means ‘blowing snow.’ A swordsman was said to test a fine blade by laying a hair on the edge and blowing it apart—but what this one blows from his blade is not snow, it is blood. Ximen Chuixue is among the great swordsmen of Gu Long’s world, and his cold devotion to the sword, purifying himself before a killing as for a holy office, is fixed in this first glimpse of him.

The jianghu (literally ‘rivers and lakes’) is the free-floating world in which these stories move: the society of wandering swordsmen, sects, escorts, thieves and outlaws that stands apart from settled town-and-magistrate life, with its own codes of honour, reputation and revenge. Much of what the characters do makes sense only by its rules.

The Nine Provinces (jiuzhou) were the divisions into which legend split the realm of the sage-kings; the name stands poetically for all of China. In the original the boast runs to exactly five characters—yi dao zhen jiu zhou, ‘one blade quells the Nine Provinces’—which is the point of the tally that follows: five characters, one life. (Chinese counts by the written character where English counts by the word.)

Another name-play. Hua Manlou reads literally as ‘flowers fill the tower,’ and the vignette opens by turning the name back into a picture: fresh flowers filling his upper room. Blind since childhood, gentle and quietly formidable, he is the third of the swordsmen introduced here and Lu Xiaofeng’s closest friend.

His swagger rests on two puns. Taisui—here ‘Terror’—is the dreaded star-deity Grand Duke Jupiter, whose name became slang for a local strongman no one dares cross (‘to break ground over Taisui’s head’ is to court ruin). And his given name, Yidong, means literally ‘one hole’—hence his boast that one stroke of his blade will leave one more hole in you, and Hua Manlou’s dry answer that he wants no more holes of any size.

The guqin is the seven-stringed zither of the Chinese scholar, played softly for one’s own ear and long the emblem of cultivation and inward calm. That a blind man alone in a tower should count it among his contentments is of a piece with everything else he says here.

The riddle that names the book’s hero and titles its first chapter. Lu Xiaofeng wears a moustache whose two upswept tips read like a second pair of eyebrows—hence ‘four eyebrows.’ The answer is withheld here on purpose; Hua Manlou’s friend is about to walk into the story proper.

ch01.anchor: taken for all he was worth
ch01.note: A gambler’s superstition explains the old man’s dread. To meet a monk on the way to play was reckoned a sure sign you would lose everything: the omen turns on the monk’s shaved, hairless head—guang, ‘bare, cleaned bald’—and the gambler’s word for being wiped out, shu guang, ‘to lose until you are stripped clean.’ The same belief lies behind the passengers’ curse, a little later, that crossing a monk brings foul luck.

ch02.note: Wangba (王八) is one of the coarser Chinese insults: literally ‘tortoise,’ used interchangeably with 乌龟, and long ago fixed as the standing slang for a cheating scoundrel and above all a cuckolded husband. It runs through the whole scene ahead. The graffiti scrawled across the four bound men’s brows below (one a turtle, one a wangba, the others a ‘live pig’ and a ‘country cur’) trades on the same word twice over. So does the closing gag when the scarred man tosses an empty green wine jar onto the wangba-labelled head, since in Chinese folk-thought a cuckold’s mark is a green cap (lümaozi, 绿帽子). And the exchange further on between Lu Xiaofeng and the Boss’s Wife about ‘live cuckolds’ and ‘dead cuckolds’ is the same joke in yet another key.

The wuxia stock trick called dianxue (点穴): a martial artist strikes a specific acupuncture point on his opponent’s body to freeze the limb, seal off the voice, or immobilise the whole man for hours. It is treated throughout this fiction as an ordinary battlefield skill; the reader will meet it many times.

The rooms of a good Chinese inn were graded by the opening characters of the classical primer, the Thousand-Character Text: tian di xuan huang (天地玄黄), ‘heaven, earth, black, yellow.’ The Heaven Room (天字号房) was the best in the house.

Yingchun (迎春) is literally ‘welcoming the spring,’ and ‘spring’ is the standard Chinese poetic euphemism for erotic feeling. A house so named is a brothel; here, the best-appointed one in Huangshi Town.

ch02.anchor: a hundred and eight of them
ch02.note: The number 108 is deeply grounded in Chinese Buddhist and secular tradition — 108 beads on the rosary, 108 defilements in the mind of man, 108 outlaws in the Water Margin. The Blue-Robe Tower’s 108-fold structure sits inside that inheritance, and Lu Xiaofeng’s threat below to torch ‘all one hundred and eight’ of the towers is meant to hit the number as well as the buildings. The Tower itself is Gu Long’s invention.

ch02.anchor: The one with the scar was called the Iron-Faced Judge
ch02.note: Panguan (判官), rendered here ‘Judge,’ is not the magistrate of law-court fiction but the underworld clerk of the Ten Courts of Hell, who reads out the ledger of a soul’s deeds before the King of the Dead pronounces sentence. Iron pens in the shape of writing brushes are the panguan’s traditional weapon, and give this thug both his epithet and his signature blades. When he is later hurled out through the window ‘off to meet the real Judge,’ the pun folds shut.

Pan Jinlian (潘金莲) is the fatally beautiful adulteress of the sixteenth-century novels Water Margin (Shuihu zhuan) and The Golden Lotus (Jin Ping Mei); Ximen Qing (西门庆) is her wealthy libertine seducer. The Boss’s Wife accuses Lu of casting her in the adulteress’s role; his reply — ‘even if you were Pan Jinlian, I’m no Ximen Qing’ — turns the joke on the shared surname Ximen, the same one carried by his fellow swordsman Ximen Chuixue (Prologue).

Liu Xiahui (柳下惠), a nobleman of the state of Lu in the seventh century BC, is proverbial in China for chastity: the story runs that he once sat all night with a woman on his lap in the freezing cold to warm her, and never took an improper thought. To call a man ‘a Liu Xiahui’ is to call him incorruptible in the presence of a beautiful woman — here, said with heavy sarcasm.

Split-crotch trousers (kaidangku, 开裆裤) are the traditional garment of the Chinese toddler, a pair open at the seat so the child can relieve himself without help. ‘To have known each other since split-crotch pants’ is the standing Chinese idiom for a friendship going back to earliest childhood.

ch02.anchor: Love, from of old, leaves only regret behind
ch02.note: A couplet in the vernacular tradition — found in popular verse and used freely by Gu Long — which puns on the ravaged man’s name. Liu Yuhen (柳余恨) reads literally as ‘Liu — only regret is left’; the first line, duoqing zigu kong yu hen (多情自古空余恨), buries his given name in itself: ‘the passionate always leave only regret behind.’ It is his own name, and his own life, that he is quoting when he says the Jade-Faced Gentleman is dead.

ch02.anchor: Autumn wind, autumn rain — enough to sicken a man to death
ch02.note: A famous line — the last poem, so tradition holds, of the young revolutionary Qiu Jin (秋瑾), written just before her execution in 1907 — recycled here as the killer’s private motto. It puns on his name too: Xiao Qiuyu (萧秋雨) reads as ‘Xiao — autumn rain.’ Gu Long is playful with such literary quotations, and his solitary killers are often given the diction of scholars.

ch03.note: A play on Lu Xiaofeng’s name. The princess is Danfeng (丹凤), ‘scarlet phoenix’; Lu’s given name Xiaofeng (小凤) is ‘little phoenix.’ The child is correcting him: it is Princess Scarlet-Phoenix who has come, not some Princess named after him. Her surname, and the whole royal house’s, proves to be Shangguan — the same borne by Shangguan Feiyan of the Prologue.

A pun that does not survive into English. Chinese jiugui (酒鬼), literally ‘wine-ghost,’ is the everyday word for a drunkard. Told there is a ‘ghost’ (gui) in the jar that will not break, Dugu Fang answers that it is of course a wine-ghost — a sot — the only kind of ghost a wine-jar would keep.

Lu You (陆游, 1125–1210), styled Fangweng (放翁, ‘the old man set free’), was among the best-loved poets of the Southern Song and a fervent patriot, of whose verses thousands survive. He shares the surname Lu with Lu Xiaofeng, but no kinship is implied: the whole speech is Lu Xiaofeng inventing a priceless pedigree for a plain hut in order to fleece the child, and the ‘master craftsman Lu Zhi’ a few lines earlier is very likely invented too.

ch03.anchor: Lust is a blade that scrapes the bone
ch03.note: A well-worn folk couplet — se shi guagu gangdao, jiu shi chuanchang duyao (色是刮骨钢刀，酒是穿肠毒药), ‘lust is a steel knife that scrapes the bone, wine a poison that pierces the gut’ — from the moralising tradition that warns against the four vices of wine, lust, wealth and wrath. Xiao Qiuyu quotes it drily as his warrant for smashing the jars.

ch04.anchor: Then why did you come to the Central Lands
ch04.note: Zhongtu (中土), ‘the central land,’ is China proper, the settled agrarian heartland, named here from the vantage of a frontier people for whom it is the centre of the civilised world. The kingdom of the Golden Roc lies somewhere out beyond its western marches.

The Cossacks — horse-borne warrior communities of the Eurasian steppe, north of the Black and Caspian Seas — are an anachronism here, of a piece with Gu Long’s deliberately vague, half-legendary geography. Their mention places the fallen kingdom of the Golden Roc far out on the north-western frontier, beyond the passes, among the powers of the steppe.

Mount Emei (峨嵋) in Sichuan is one of the sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism; in martial-arts fiction it is also the seat of a great sword-school, a pillar of the jianghu beside Shaolin and Wudang. That its upright and public master should secretly be the traitor Dugu Yihe is the very scandal the Great King’s demand would lay bare.

A spirit-tablet (灵位, lingwei) is an inscribed wooden tablet that houses the soul of the dead for veneration; it stands on the ancestral altar and receives offerings and the reporting of family affairs. To repent one’s crime before the old King’s tablet is to make confession directly to his spirit.

Shaolin (少林), the Chan Buddhist monastery on Mount Song in Henan, and Wudang (武当), the Taoist mountain in Hubei, are the two most storied martial traditions of Chinese fiction — the Buddhist ‘hard, outer’ and Taoist ‘soft, inner’ schools. Lu Xiaofeng is naming the handful of men he reckons to have reached the summit of the martial arts; that Huo Xiu and Dugu Yihe stand among them is the measure of how formidable the Great King’s two chief enemies are.

An allusion to the classic novel Water Margin, in which the innkeepers Sun Erniang and Zhang Qing drug lone travellers with knock-out wine and grind the bodies into the stuffing of steamed buns (renrou baozi, 人肉包子). Lu Xiaofeng’s closing joke — that he hopes the night’s fare is not man-flesh buns, nor the drink a soul-stealing wine — casts the eerie, half-empty mansion of the Golden Roc as just such a bandit inn.
